		<title>E-Series GPU IP: The First Step Towards Converged Acceleration</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/e-series-gpu-ip-the-first-step-towards-converged-acceleration/</link>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Combine graphics, compute and AI on one flexible architecture and one programmable software stack, with up to 32 TOPS Int8 per core at 1GHz and the ability to run graphics and AI workloads concurrently.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/e-series-gpu-ip-the-first-step-towards-converged-acceleration/">E-Series GPU IP: The First Step Towards Converged Acceleration</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p class="wp-block-paragraph">E-Series, announced in 2025 and with first silicon expected by the end of 2026, marks a new era for edge system design. E-Series combines graphics, compute and AI on one flexible architecture and one programmable software stack.   With up to 32 TOPS Int8 per core at 1GHz (4× the raw compute performance of D-Series) and the ability to run graphics and AI workloads concurrently, E-Series provides system designers with:</p>
<ul class="wp-block-list">
<li>Advanced graphics acceleration for the latest games and user interfaces.</li>
<li>A flexible co-processor that can offload dedicated AI processors at peak times.</li>
<li>A general-purpose accelerator that can be trusted to run the operators of the future as AI models evolve.</li>
</ul>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph"><strong>This paper includes chapters on:</strong></p>
<ul class="wp-block-list">
<li>The convergence of edge processors.</li>
<li>The E-Series GPU architecture.</li>
<li>How E-Series delivers edge-level power efficiency.</li>
<li>Real-world performance data for E-Series across gaming, neural rendering and language models.</li>
<li>A look at the E-Series software stack.</li>
</ul>
<p>Read <a href="https://www.imaginationtech.com/resources/e-series-the-first-step-towards-converged-acceleration/">more here</a>.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async" class="alignnone wp-image-24282084" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-29-at-11.21.22-AM.png?resize=487%2C487&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="487" height="487" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-29-at-11.21.22-AM.png?resize=300%2C300&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-29-at-11.21.22-AM.png?resize=150%2C150&amp;ssl=1 150w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-29-at-11.21.22-AM.png?resize=768%2C766&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-29-at-11.21.22-AM.png?resize=600%2C599&amp;ssl=1 600w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-29-at-11.21.22-AM.png?resize=100%2C100&amp;ssl=1 100w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-29-at-11.21.22-AM.png?resize=24%2C24&amp;ssl=1 24w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-29-at-11.21.22-AM.png?resize=48%2C48&amp;ssl=1 48w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-29-at-11.21.22-AM.png?resize=96%2C96&amp;ssl=1 96w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-29-at-11.21.22-AM.png?w=804&amp;ssl=1 804w" sizes="(max-width: 487px) 100vw, 487px" /></p>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Bridging the gap between open-source Root of Trust foundations and enterprise-grade security deployments.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/from-caliptra-foundation-to-full-production-deployment/">From Caliptra Foundation To Full Production Deployment</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<div class="row-fluid-wrapper row-depth-1 row-number-4 ">
<div class="row-fluid ">
<div class="span12 widget-span widget-type-widget_container ">
<div id="hs_cos_wrapper_module_13885047978573602" class="hs_cos_wrapper hs_cos_wrapper_widget hs_cos_wrapper_type_rich_text" data-id="40381" data-hml-enabled="1">
<p>As AI infrastructure and modern data centers become increasingly dependent on heterogeneous processors, accelerators, and controllers, establishing trust in every device has become a critical security requirement. This white paper examines how the open-source Caliptra Root of Trust framework provides a common foundation for device identity, measured boot, and attestation across data center-class systems, while highlighting the challenges and means of transforming an open standard into a production-ready deployment. By enabling organizations to preserve alignment with the Caliptra ecosystem while accelerating deployment and reducing integration risk, a practical path from open-source Root of Trust adoption to enterprise-grade security implementation for data center and AI infrastructure can be realized.</p>
</div>
</div>
</div>
</div>

<div class="cell-wrapper layout-widget-wrapper" data-id="40384" data-hml-enabled="1">
<h2>Learn:</h2>
<ul>
<li>Why Caliptra is emerging as a common Root of Trust foundation for data center and AI infrastructure security</li>
<li>The challenges of turning an open-source Root of Trust into a production-ready, certifiable commercial deployment</li>
<li>How CryptoManager Root of Trust for use with the Caliptra specification extends trust across the SoC while preserving Caliptra ecosystem alignment and trademark</li>
</ul>
<p><a href="https://go.rambus.com/from-caliptra-foundation-to-full-production-deployment">Read more here.</a></p>

<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/make-your-interface-work-for-your-ai-soc-a-10-step-program-ip-solutions-and-models/">Make Your Interface Work For Your AI SoC—A 10 Step Program: IP Solutions And Models</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>AI-driven SoCs are placing unprecedented demands on compute, memory, and connectivity, making interfaces such as PCIe, CXL, Ethernet, HBM, USB, and UFS critical to overall system performance and verification success. As software and hardware complexity continue to increase, development teams need verification strategies that span simulation, hardware-assisted verification, virtual prototyping, and silicon validation to reduce risk and accelerate time-to-market.</p>
<p>This white paper examines how to establish a foundation for comprehensive hardware-software verification and validation. Learn how proven IP, verification solutions, and virtual platforms enable earlier software development, improve interoperability, and streamline deployment of complex AI SoCs and multi-die systems.</p>
<p>Learn:</p>
<ul>
<li>Why Interface IP, PHY integration, and Verification IP are essential for achieving protocol compliance, interoperability, and reliable system integration.</li>
</ul>
<ul>
<li>How hardware-assisted verification using emulation and prototyping platforms helps uncover rare protocol issues, long-duration failures, and software-driven corner cases before silicon.</li>
</ul>
<ul>
<li>How virtual models and transaction-level platforms enable parallel hardware and software development, accelerating bring-up and reducing project risk.</li>
</ul>
<ul>
<li>Best practices for creating a continuous verification strategy that spans architectural exploration, software development, simulation, hardware-assisted verification, and post-silicon validation.</li>
</ul>
<p><a href="https://www.synopsys.com/resources/make-your-interface-work-10-step-program-ip-models.html">Read more here</a>.</p>

		<title>Designing Physical AI Systems Under Real-World Constraints</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/designing-physical-ai-systems-under-real-world-constraints/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/designing-physical-ai-systems-under-real-world-constraints/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Cadence]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Wed, 30 Sep 2026 07:02:34 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[IoT and Security]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Whitepapers]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Cadence]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[data movement]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[edge]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[edge AI]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[physical AI]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[sensors]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24282137</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Where latency, power, reliability, and data movement shape system behavior.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/designing-physical-ai-systems-under-real-world-constraints/">Designing Physical AI Systems Under Real-World Constraints</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<div class="richtext section">
<div class="expandable-refresh expandable-collapse">
<div class="expandable-wrapper">
<div class="expandable-content">
<p>Physical AI extends artificial intelligence into systems that sense, interpret, and act in the physical world. Unlike centralized AI infrastructure, these systems operate within bounded latency, power, thermal, reliability, and environmental constraints. They must respond to changing inputs in real time, often under conditions where delayed or inconsistent behavior can affect equipment, processes, or human safety.</p>
<p>While Physical AI often operates at the edge, it extends beyond edge AI by combining AI inference with closed-loop interaction in the physical world, where sensing, decision-making, and actuation operate together under strict timing and operational constraints.</p>
<p>At the center of Physical AI is a continuous sensing, inference, and response cycle. Sensor data is captured, processed, interpreted, and translated into action. Maintaining that cycle requires predictable behavior across memory, compute, communication, and I/O resources. Delays in data arrival, variability in memory access, inefficient communication, or synchronization overhead can directly affect how the system responds.</p>
<p>Physical AI systems must move, process, and act on data within strict timing and operational constraints. Memory, communication, synchronization, and I/O are all part of the control path.</p>
<p>Edge AI plays a central role in this architecture because many Physical AI systems cannot rely on centralized infrastructure for immediate decisions. Sensor data may be too large, too frequent, too latency-sensitive, or too safety-critical to send to a remote system before action is taken. Local execution becomes necessary, but edge environments introduce additional constraints, including limited power budgets, thermal variation, vibration, motion, shock, humidity, and other physical operating conditions.</p>
<p>These infrastructure constraints are implemented through silicon-level decisions. Memory interfaces, interconnect, I/O subsystems, and die-to-die links carry, exchange, and synchronize data across the system.</p>
<p>Physical AI systems also rarely operate in isolation. Devices often participate in larger architectures spanning edge, industrial, vehicle, and cloud environments, where information must be exchanged and coordinated across multiple system boundaries. The same data movement, synchronization, and infrastructure challenges extend beyond a single device and shape behavior across the broader system.</p>
</div>
<div class="dividerModule section"><a href="https://www.cadence.com/en_US/home/resources/white-papers/designing-physical-ai-systems-under-real-world-constraints.html">Read more here</a>.</div>

		<title>PCIe 8.0 Over UCIe 3.0: Bringing A Proven Protocol Into The Chiplet Era</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/pcie-8-0-over-ucie-3-0-bringing-a-proven-rrotocol-into-the-chiplet-era/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/pcie-8-0-over-ucie-3-0-bringing-a-proven-rrotocol-into-the-chiplet-era/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Siemens EDA]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Wed, 30 Sep 2026 07:02:19 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[IoT and Security]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>UCIe standardizes die-to-die communication within a package and allows PCIe traffic to traverse chiplet boundaries with seamless interoperability over standardized interconnects.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/pcie-8-0-over-ucie-3-0-bringing-a-proven-rrotocol-into-the-chiplet-era/">PCIe 8.0 Over UCIe 3.0: Bringing A Proven Protocol Into The Chiplet Era</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>As architectures move from monolithic SoCs to chiplet-based designs, the value of PCIe remains high, yet conventional PCIe implementations board-oriented assumptions are no longer ideal for short-reach, in-package communication.</p>
<p>UCIe standardizes die-to-die communication within a package and allows PCIe traffic to traverse chiplet boundaries with seamless interoperability over standardized interconnects.</p>
<p>For PCIe 8.0, this approach enables high bandwidth with better transport efficiency, enhanced modularity, and stronger scalability for AI, HPC, and heterogeneous compute systems.</p>
<p>Ready to dive deeper into the future of chiplet-based designs and discover how UCIe is revolutionizing PCIe for AI, HPC, and heterogeneous compute systems?</p>
<p><a href="https://resources.sw.siemens.com/en-US/white-paper-pcie-8-0-over-ucie-3-0-bringing-a-proven-protocol-into-the-chiplet-era/">Read more here</a>.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Enabling silicon to operate closer to its true performance envelope without excessive guard banding. </p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/data-center-energy-trends-force-a-rethink-of-chip-power-delivery/">Data Center Energy Trends Force A Rethink Of Chip Power Delivery</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p><strong>By Kaladhar Radhakrishnan, Vishal Javvaji, and Nicolas Butzen</strong></p>
<p>The modern data center is facing a sharp uptick in power consumption driven by the rapid growth of AI, high-performance computing (HPC), and cloud-scale services. The training of large models, real-time inference, and data-intensive applications are driving unprecedented compute density and current demands.</p>
<p>According to Gartner, “worldwide data center power demand is expected to rise 27% in 2026 and reach 132 gigawatts (GW), up from 104GW in 2025. It is estimated to attain 290GW by 2030, which reflects the unprecedented scale and pace of GenAI boosting demand.” AI-optimized servers continue to fuel the increase in data center power consumption. Gartner estimates “AI-optimized server adoption will account for 31% of data center power consumption in 2026, and that by 2027 their power consumption will surpass that of conventional servers.”¹</p>
<p>In our latest <a href="https://www.intel.com/content/dam/www/central-libraries/us/en/documents/2026-08/foundry-power-delivery-white-paper.pdf">technical white paper</a>, we take a deep dive into how power delivery is becoming one of the dominant forces shaping how systems are architected, deployed, and scaled.</p>
<h2>Traditional power delivery constraints</h2>
<p>Power efficiency is often viewed as a system-on-chip (SoC) design challenge, but in modern AI and cloud data centers, the real constraints extend well beyond the silicon itself.  Nearly all projected growth in electricity demand comes from AI infrastructure and the additional cooling and support systems required to operate it. Rack-level power limits, facility power budgets, and cooling capacity increasingly dictate how much compute can be deployed, making every watt a critical resource shared across processors, memory, networking, and storage.</p>
<p>At the same time, conventional frontside power delivery imposes a growing tax on silicon efficiency. By routing power and signals through the same metal layers, traditional architectures force competition for valuable routing resources. These challenges are further amplified by rising current demands and shrinking voltage margins. Even small increases in resistance and inductance can degrade power integrity and lead to timing failures. Designers compensate through wider power rails, additional decoupling, and larger guard bands, adding cost and complexity while delivering diminishing returns.</p>
<h2>Decoupling power and signal routing</h2>
<p>Intel Foundry is addressing these challenges with backside power delivery architectures that move power routing off the signal layers, improving routing efficiency, reducing IR drop, and enhancing performance-per-watt at advanced process nodes. Introduced with Intel 18A, RibbonFET Gate-all-around (GAA) transistor architecture with PowerVia technology makes power delivery an enabling foundation for performance.</p>
<p>At the top end of the device portfolio, RibbonFET with Power Boost is a performance optimized dual contact device option engineered to increase available drive current through mobility enhancements and ultra-low resistance contacts, translating directly into higher achievable frequency at matched capacitance on Intel 18A-P. PowerDirect, the second generation of Intel Foundry’s backside power delivery technology planned for Intel 14A, will build on the benefits of PowerVia by introducing additional area efficiencies and a more optimized power delivery architecture, further improving overall power, performance, and area (PPA).</p>
<h2>A new power delivery architecture</h2>
<p>In a backside power delivery architecture, power is delivered physically closer to the transistors that consume it. Shorter vertical power paths reduce resistance and inductance, directly lowering IR drop and improving voltage stability. PowerVia anchors this architecture by supplying power through dedicated backside layers, while Intel Foundry’s capacitor technologies — Omni MIM (a high-density on die metal-insulator-metal capacitor) and substrate embedded MIM with through-silicon vias (eMIM-T) — provide dense, efficient near-load decoupling to support stable operation. Together, these elements allow silicon to operate closer to its true performance envelope without excessive guard banding.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282120" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Intel_Data-Center-Energy-Chip-Power-Delivery-fig1.webp?resize=1372%2C792&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1372" height="792" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Intel_Data-Center-Energy-Chip-Power-Delivery-fig1.webp?w=1372&amp;ssl=1 1372w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Intel_Data-Center-Energy-Chip-Power-Delivery-fig1.webp?resize=300%2C173&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Intel_Data-Center-Energy-Chip-Power-Delivery-fig1.webp?resize=1024%2C591&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Intel_Data-Center-Energy-Chip-Power-Delivery-fig1.webp?resize=768%2C443&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Intel_Data-Center-Energy-Chip-Power-Delivery-fig1.webp?resize=600%2C346&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 1: Backside power delivery using PowerVia (Omni MIM spotlight on left).</strong></p>
<p>This proximity becomes especially critical for modern bursty workloads such as AI inference and HPC acceleration, where current demand shifts rapidly over short time scales. Shorter power paths enable faster transient response, reducing droop during workload spikes and improving overall energy efficiency. Technologies such as embedded deep trench capacitors (eDTC) further strengthen localized charge delivery, while advanced packaging solutions like Embedded Multi-die Interconnect Bridge-T (EMIB-T) extend these benefits across multi‑die systems with high‑bandwidth, low‑loss interconnects. The result is a power delivery architecture designed to handle dynamic, power‑dense computing workloads driving today’s data centers.</p>
<p>By moving power closer to the transistors and pairing it with dense, localized decoupling and system‑scale extensions, backside power delivery breaks the escalating trade‑offs between performance, efficiency, and reliability that constrain traditional designs. The result is not just cleaner power, but greater architectural freedom: tighter margins without fragility, higher utilization without excessive guard bands, and scalability without disproportionate complexity.</p>
<p>Read our <a href="https://www.intel.com/content/dam/www/central-libraries/us/en/documents/2026-08/foundry-power-delivery-white-paper.pdf">technical white paper</a> to dive deeper into how Intel Foundry’s power delivery solutions can help scale your designs.</p>

		<title>Switch Faster, Regulate Faster, Protect Faster With Performance Line Microcontrollers</title>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>How high-speed control, precision timing, and hardware acceleration enable next-gen PSUs, IBCs, and BBUs.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/switch-faster-regulate-faster-protect-faster-with-performance-line-microcontrollers/">Switch Faster, Regulate Faster, Protect Faster With Performance Line Microcontrollers</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>AI data center power design has entered a new phase, but it does comes with challenges. The first challenge is architectural: how to move enough power into dense AI racks efficiently. The next challenge is control: How to switch faster, regulate faster, protect faster, and still keep the firmware architecture manageable. In power supply units (PSUs), intermediate bus converters (IBCs), and battery backup units (BBUs), GaN and SiC power stages are pushing switching frequencies higher while AI workloads are demanding faster dynamic response from every conversion stage.</p>
<p>This white paper continues the discussion from Empowering AI Power Supply Innovation with PSOC Control C3 Performance Line. Instead of revisiting the rack-level power architecture trends, it focuses on the microcontroller features that make high-frequency digital power practical: the Programmable Power Control Accelerator (PPCA), 25 MSPS ADC subsystem, sub-100 ps high-resolution PWM, comparators with slope generation, hardware 3P3Z filters, Custom Logic Block, Event Processing Unit, PMBus and CAN FD interfaces, safety libraries, and security capabilities. The goal is to help power designers connect system-level pain points to silicon-level solutions.</p>
<p>When a PSU must run an interleaved PFC stage and an LLC stage, when an IBC must regulate a 48 V or high-voltage intermediate bus close to the load, or when a BBU must transition between charge, discharge, ORing, and protection states, PSOC Control C3 Performance Line microcontrollers (MCUs) provide a control architecture built for the timing, sensing, and compute requirements of modern data center power.</p>
<p>Read <a href="https://www.infineon.com/assets/row/public/documents/30/59/infineon-psoc-control-performance-line-switch-fast-whitepaper-en.pdf">more here</a>.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone wp-image-24282095" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-29-at-1.18.29-PM.png?resize=925%2C450&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="925" height="450" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-29-at-1.18.29-PM.png?resize=300%2C146&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-29-at-1.18.29-PM.png?resize=1024%2C499&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-29-at-1.18.29-PM.png?resize=768%2C374&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-29-at-1.18.29-PM.png?resize=600%2C292&amp;ssl=1 600w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-29-at-1.18.29-PM.png?w=1396&amp;ssl=1 1396w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 925px) 100vw, 925px" /></p>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>What it is, why it's important, and how it's impacting the movement of data.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/photonics-fundamentals-for-electronics-engineers-ebook/">Photonics Fundamentals For Electronics Engineers: eBook</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>AI has created a crisis in the data center. The amount of data that needs to be processed and stored has pushed compute and memory density far beyond what anyone thought possible even a few years ago. But how to move that data back and forth quickly and efficiently between processors and memory remains a work in progress.</p>
<p>While the chip industry was built around the ability to move electrons through wires, there has long been a recognition that at some point photons would become the better choice for moving data at, well, the speed of light. That time has finally arrived.</p>
<p>Still, what sounds good in theory has proved to be far more complicated in practice. Just plugging optical cables into server racks was considered revolutionary a decade ago. Harnessing light, controlling its movement, protecting signals from various types of noise, and translating signals from electrical to optical and back to electrical were the stuff of science fiction.</p>
<p>Many elements and technologies are required to enable optical data movement. So far, most of the focus has been on connections between servers in a rack, and between racks, but in the future optical signals will move to the package level, and eventually much closer to where data is actually processed.</p>
<p>This eBook offers insights into what&#8217;s involved in photonics design, what&#8217;s changing (or at least what we know so far), and how those changes will affect semiconductor and electronic design in the future.</p>
<p><strong>Click on the first image below</strong> to read the photonics eBook.</p>
